Title: When confusion reigns, trusted vendors must guide their SMB customers
Context: Phishing, vulnerability exploitation, infostealers, compromised credentials, and business email compromise (BEC) are still among the most popular avenues for threat actors
Full Text:
Cybersecurity for smaller businesses often suffers by being either underpowered or too complex. This tension can be challenging to resolve for small IT teams that may lack an in-house cyber expert. Understanding the problem is not the same as understanding where the solution lies.

Effective SMB protection demands that vendors lead their customers through a clear onboarding process – and offer practical and transparent guidance during incident response engagements.

Without trusted partnerships like this, SMBs may struggle to optimize the way they use security products and services. They may find it difficult to explain incidents to insurers and regulators. And they may fail to learn from threat events in a way that can help to build long-term resilience.

Complexity is everywhere

These challenges are important not just for SMBs themselves to overcome. As they make up over 99% of all private sector companies in Europe and North America, small and mid-sized firms are the backbone of most economies and comprise the supply chain of larger organizations. That puts them directly in the firing line of threat actors looking for weaknesses to probe, en route to client data or network access. Production outages at critical points in supply chains can have potentially catastrophic knock-on effects.

Fortunately, SMB IT and security leaders get it and increasingly consider cybersecurity very or extremely important. That may be because many organizations have suffered at least one cyber incident in the past 12 months alone. These events tend to focus the mind, particularly when they’re significant or critical and lead to system downtime, data breaches, ransomware, email compromise, and more.

But awareness and action are two different things. SMBs know they need effective protection, but their efforts to achieve this often hit a familiar roadblock: complexity. Many often say that even keeping up with the latest trends and threats is a major challenge. The speed with which the threat landscape changes is just one of many contributing factors.

At a basic level, security best practices remain broadly the same, as do the types of threat that businesses can expect. Phishing, vulnerability exploitation, infostealers, compromised credentials, and business email compromise (BEC) are still among the most popular avenues for threat actors. AI merely amplifies and accelerates. However, peel back the onion a layer or two and threat intelligence can become intimidatingly complex.

Understanding what a genuine threat to the organization is and what not to worry about is often beyond the capability of a small IT security team. They might have neither the time nor subject matter expertise to make an effective assessment. Security often suffers as a result, becoming reactive and piecemeal.

Vendors can make life harder

The cybersecurity market can compound these challenges. The sheer variety of solutions and services on offer is staggering. It’s a global market worth an estimated $248 billion, rising potentially to $699 billion by 2034. This can make it difficult to compare vendor offerings effectively, even if they’re nominally in the same category. And once purchased, some solutions can be challenging for less-skilled teams to configure and operate. Getting the right fit for your business is critical.

Over half (55%) of SMBs surveyed by ESET argue that the cybersecurity solutions market is confusing and complicated, while nearly a third (30%) say solution complexity is a major challenge. The language used by the industry can also be impenetrable. Around three-quarters (72%) want plain-language explanations. Many don’t know the meaning of widely used monikers like MDR, EDR and XDR.

The pathway to supervised support

Yet there is some clarity among this confusion. SMBs know that preventative security is important. But they also realize that in some circumstances threat actors will always get through those defenses. That’s why most businesses ESET speaks to want protection that goes beyond ‘antivirus’ (AV) and essential safeguards.

This extra layer of protection should function as advanced support for specialized threats, complementing in-house management of basic security controls. Basic solutions will block malicious executables, for example, but what about sophisticated threat actors living off the land using safe-looking tools? Or an AI-discovered zero-day exploit for which there is no signature? Detecting these threats is the power of services like MDR.

The challenge is that they don’t work out of the box. Their effectiveness depends on how well a provider’s people, processes, and technology are aligned with your environment. Coverage is essential, as gaps can mean potential blind spots that hackers can exploit. If any exist, they should be well documented and regularly reviewed as your IT environment continues to evolve.

Visibility must also extend to the tooling that you have in place. Every organization is different. That means specialist MDR teams must clarify at onboarding the specific IT setup of the client, so they can quickly spot if an unsanctioned tool (like remote monitoring software) appears, which may indicate malicious activity.

All of which makes onboarding and setup a vital first step in a successful MDR engagement.

What guided onboarding should include

Most SMBs want step-by-step guidance on setting up a new cybersecurity product or service. This will ensure it’s integrated seamlessly into day-to-day operations. But what should that onboarding include?

A live onboarding session with a vendor expert provides a great opportunity to ask questions as you’re being onboarded. Technical documentation is useful to refer to in some circumstances. But it can easily become overwhelming for less-skilled IT professionals. That’s why a live on-to-one session is invaluable; helping you to fill in the gaps with plain English explanations and learn through doing, not reading.

Activation of the environment ensures it’s all up and running and helps you get an early look and feel of what to expect.

Configuration and readiness checks are critical to ensure the service is optimized to work with your environment. Activation is just the first step. Configuration gets it operational. These checks are important to do during guided onboarding as they may be challenging for a non-specialist team to perform on its own.

Guidance on notification, reporting and communication is about helping you understand how alerts will come through and how reporting is handled. You’ll learn who gets the notifications on your side and what will be expected of them when they do. It’s vital to get this right in order to prevent communication gaps between your team members and between your team and the vendor.

An all-in-one installer can help to streamline deployment across all relevant endpoints, minimizing the configuration workload, and reducing time and human error.

Running through MDR operations, incident workflows and reporting is about understanding how your vendor partner investigates and communicates incidents, and how to interpret reports. It’s about setting expectations on what your responsibilities are once the provider has identified an incident. Few vendors will take care of the entire incident and remediation workflow so knowing what’s expected of your team is critically important.

A final set of best practices and next-step suggestions will shape your understanding of how to maintain the service over time, as the IT environment and threat landscape change. Prioritizing what matters most once you’re up and running is useful for teams with few resources who are committed to continuous improvement.

Above all, remember that the engineer is there to guide you through the process, not do all the heavy lifting themself. It’s about giving you the know-how to make the partnership a success, and optimize your use of the product or service.

When done correctly, it should mean faster time to protection, a lower risk of misconfiguration, and improved confidence that you can get the most out of your investment.

Guidance during use

Once you’re up and running, a good vendor should guide you through the process of incident detection and response. That means helping you to understand:

What happened: Explaining an incident in plain English. What kind of threat was detected. Which IT systems were affected. How the adversary gained initial access. Whether data was compromised or stolen. And what remains unclear.

Why it matters: Your vendor should help by translating technical into business risks. That will help you understand what the implications are for the organization, rather than thinking solely in IT terms. For example, a vulnerability exploitation may have enabled access to a customer database, which could raise the prospect of data loss and a GDPR investigation.

What the provider did: Your security partner should detail exactly what steps it took to investigate and contain the threat, such as resetting passwords or isolating accounts. And what has yet to be done.

What happens next: This is the most important part of the guidance. Your provider should provide actionable next steps, ideally in order of importance. It could include patching an exploited system, enabling MFA, restoring data from backups, etc. These recommendations should be clear, including who is responsible and ideal timelines. Because when intrusions happen, minutes matter.

They should also contain supporting evidence such as logs that can be used to share with auditors, regulators and insurers if required. And to inform any customer outreach or business continuity efforts (such as restarting systems) that may be required. Evidence is also essential to minimize the chances of a similar incident occurring again. Resilience is all about learning the lessons of each intrusion to close off potential pathways for future threats.

Transparency is critical

If SMBs don’t receive this kind of clarity and detail during live incidents, there’s a risk that they may mistakenly believe malicious activity has been remediated, when in fact there is work left to do to contain and resolve the issue. That can allow the blast radius of an attack to spread, causing more damage.

Customers, regulators and other stakeholders might also remain in the dark, creating extra reputational and financial risk. And the organization itself will not have the forensic knowledge to hand to improve cyber resilience going forward.

Fundamentally, if you’re unable to determine what actions your provider took, you can’t calculate whether their service is worth the money you’re paying for it.

The value of human relationships

SMBs understand the value of cybersecurity. And they know that the threat landscape is becoming more volatile, potentially imperilling their business. But those without sufficient expertise are frustrated by the “known unknowns” that prevent them from understanding how the latest threats and trends affect their organization.

This is where security vendors must step up. They are trusted by more SMBs than any other entity – including internal staff, industry peers, and governments – as a trusted source of cybersecurity guidance.

SMBs don’t want to hand over all control for threat protection. They want to be empowered by trusted partners to keep their business more secure. At the center of this dynamic sit human relationships – and we know that SMBs value access to a human expert.

The key for vendors is to ensure these experts are available at onboarding, to guide SMBs through configuration, activation and setup. And that they’re on hand during incident response, to explain what happened, why it matters, what steps have been taken, and what there is left to do. It’s the kind of supervised protection that could turn cybersecurity from a cost of doing business into a true growth enabler for SMBs.

Title: Amatera: How the prolific infostealer works and spreads
Context: ESET detections jumped by more than 500% in the first half of 2025 compared with the previous six months, making it the second most common attack vector after phishing
Full Text:
Infostealers have become an established business, with developers who produce and maintain the product and paying customers who run their own campaigns with them. Amatera – which topped ESET’s infostealer detections in Latin America in the first half of 2026 but targets victims worldwide – shows what this professionalization looks like in practice.

Like many other infostealers, Amatera goes after a range of data spanning login credentials, session cookies, tokens, crypto wallet information, messaging data, files, and secrets from development environments. The sheer breadth of the loot shows why infostealers are a mainstay of cybercrime – a single compromise can lead to account hijacking, financial fraud and crypto theft, as well as open the door into the organization where the victim works.

Here’s more about where Amatera came from, along with its business model, capabilities, and distribution.

What is Amatera?

Detected by ESET products as Win/PSW.Amatera, Amatera is a Windows infostealer written in C++ that was first observed in 2024. Since it’s marketed under the malware-as-a-service (MaaS) model, its developers maintain the code, the control panel, and the support infrastructure, while affiliates pay a subscription to use the malware in their campaigns.

Given the similarities in their respective code, Amatera is very likely a rebrand of ACR Stealer. Indeed, the latter has a predecessor of its own: a Sekoia investigation in May 2024 described it as an updated version of the GrMsk stealer, offered as a service on underground forums.

Rebranding – or releasing an updated version of a piece of malware under a new name – is very common across the MaaS ecosystem, particularly among ransomware operators. They sometimes sell the source code when they shut down their operations to avoid being tracked, or they update and rename it as a ‘business strategy’. In some cases, they leak it so that other malicious actors can reuse it. At any rate, by the end of 2024, Amatera Stealer was already on offer for $199 a month, with support via Telegram..

Amatera’s capabilities

Amatera extracts credentials stored in web browsers, along with cookies, browsing histories, form data, and session tokens. It can also search for and grab sensitive documents and files synced with OneDrive or SharePoint – Microsoft reported a surge in attacks on its enterprise customers between late April and mid-June 2026. Separately, Straiker found that the malware also went after cryptocurrency wallet data by manipulating the clipboard.

The malware is also under constant development, and it turns up as the final payload in a wide variety of attack chains. That variety is also typical of MaaS: the developers sell the product, and each affiliate chooses their own way to deliver it.

Amatera has spread via compromised websites, search engine ads, targeted emails, fake documents, SVG files, and ClickFix via fake CAPTCHAs. Indeed, several recent analyses of Amatera campaigns worldwide show that one of its key delivery vectors is ClickFix, a social engineering technique that was first documented in 2024 and was quickly picked up by adversaries to distribute a wide range of malware families.

Often, the victim sees a message that mimics a CAPTCHA check or a browser error and warns them of supposed technical problems that can be fixed by copying a command and running it on their computer. The victim’s own keystrokes then set the compromise in motion. The technique has moved beyond fake CAPTCHAs, however, as adversaries kept the social engineering core of ClickFix with some tweaks:

· AI-fix: Attackers build pages that impersonate legitimate AI services, including Anthropic’s Artifacts, OpenAI’s Canvas, and Microsoft Copilot Pages. The pages contain fake troubleshooting content for non-existent problems.

· CrashFix: A fake ad blocker triggers fake browser crashes and warns of data loss, pushing victims toward a malicious “quick fix.”

· ConsentFix: This variant tricks the victims into handing over their OAuth authorization tokens that open their Microsoft accounts to attackers without any password being stolen.

ClickFix-based campaigns have also used legitimate but compromised WordPress sites, among other methods. Attackers gained access to these sites through weak or stolen administrative credentials or by exploiting vulnerabilities in WordPress themes and plugins.

In Latin America, Amatera topped ESET’s infostealer detections in the first half of 2026, ahead of Formbook, Vidar, Lumma Stealer, SnakeStealer, and Rhadamanthys. ClickFix’s recent growth globally hasn’t been a straight line, however. ESET detections jumped by more than 500% in the first half of 2025 compared with the previous six months, making it the second most common attack vector after phishing. Detections fell steeply in the second half of 2025, before more than doubling in the first half of 2026 as attackers adapted the technique to new environments.

Amatera’s affiliates also buy Google ads. The Straiker research mentioned above uncovered dozens of fake install pages that were promoted through paid ads and SEO poisoning and impersonated AI and developer tools, such as Claude Code, NotebookLM, JetBrains, Comet, and Snowflake, and specifically targeted developers who use AI tools. Like AI-fix, these pages piggyback off the credibility of AI brands and share the execution chain with ClickFix.

Risks and consequences of an Amatera compromise

Based on its capabilities, these are some of the potential consequences of falling victim to Amatera:

Compromise of personal or corporate accounts through stolen passwords, cookies, and tokens

Unauthorized access to email and cloud storage

Theft of crypto assets when wallets or recovery phrases are exposed

Infrastructure compromise through SSH keys, FTP credentials, or development secrets

Installation of additional malware

Use of a compromised account for fraud, internal phishing campaigns, or further intrusions

The risk spills over to employers when the victim mixes personal and work profiles in the same web browser. A home computer may hold corporate email sessions, cloud consoles, code repositories, or HR systems. The stolen information eventually becomes a gateway that another actor can buy or exploit days later.

How to prevent and respond to an Amatera compromise

Here are a few tips for staying out of harm’s way, especially in corporate environments:

Remember that no legitimate CAPTCHA, error message, or installation guide will ask you to copy commands from a web page into the Run dialog, PowerShell, or Terminal. A search engine ad is no guarantee that a site is official. That applies equally to pages that look like they belong to a well-known AI service.

Enforce application control rules and reduce the attack surface by limiting the use of system interpreters and binaries outside their normal context.

Monitor PowerShell, Rundll32, WebDAV, unusual scheduled tasks, and the clearing of PowerShell history.

Use phishing-resistant authentication and keep browser sessions as short as business needs allow.

Separate personal and work profiles, and avoid storing secrets in the browser when a managed alternative is available.

Filter newly created sites, cloned installation pages, and downloads initiated from ads when the context doesn’t justify them.

If a compromise is confirmed, isolating the device is only the first step. From a trusted device, revoke active sessions, reset passwords, and rotate API keys, tokens, SSH credentials, and any other secrets present on the system. Also, review access to email, cloud services, repositories, and financial applications. The response must track follow-on activity, rather than stop at the initial host – documented campaigns executed additional payloads, created scheduled tasks, covered their tracks, and used legitimate system tools.

Conclusion

Amatera shows how the infostealer market works today. A developer maintains the product, and other actors distribute it via compromised websites, ads, fake AI tools, emails, or ClickFix instructions. The threat can outlive the malicious file itself, however, as passwords, cookies, session tokens, and confidential documents remain valuable even after the device has been cleaned. Stolen data can fuel both immediate fraud or later intrusions, and the rise in detections in 2026 shows attackers adopting and adapting malicious toolsets at a rapid clip.

Title: Lessons from cybersecurity Black Week
Context: In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection
Full Text:
The week leading up to October 25, 2026, was every cyber defender’s nightmare: a barrage of critical vulnerabilities in PHP and the Linux kernel, a compromised LiteLLM release, a maximum-severity flaw in GitLab, a Node.js Brotli flaw, and a certificate authority incident affecting TLS trust.

A few years ago, a backlog like this would have filled a defender’s to-do list for a whole month. In the age of AI, all of this was reported within a single “Cybersecurity Black Week,” an exceptionally eventful seven-day period amid an already turbulent Black October. AI-assisted research helped uncover at least two of these flaws: PHP2Shell and the Brotli bug. On top of the breakneck patching pace, security teams faced mounting pressure to deliver status reports to other departments, management, customers, and the media.

Beyond their severity, the issues stood out for the variety of responses they demanded. Some required emergency runtime patches and upgrades; others called for containment, credential rotation, or the replacement of outdated certificate trust bundles. In several cases, installing the latest version was only the beginning of a long remediation process.

With so many problems landing at once, the main challenge was separating real risk from hype and prioritizing accordingly. Here is our assessment.

PHP2Shell: The loudest headline, with real-world limits

PHP2Shell generated the biggest media frenzy of the lot and, with it, a major headache for security teams, prompting many organizations to take their websites offline and look for emergency fixes. The name refers to two memory-safety vulnerabilities in PHP core, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, affecting PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11. Both vulnerabilities received a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) on vulnerable PHP servers. In the highest-risk setups, a demonstrated exploit can trigger the vulnerability before application code runs, meaning application-level authentication offers no protection.

With PHP powering an estimated 69% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, government agencies in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere urged organizations to patch immediately, with some advising that affected internet-facing systems be isolated or taken offline if they could not be patched promptly. Government websites in the Netherlands, Germany, France, and other countries were temporarily taken offline as a precaution. The PHP project released fixes on October 21 in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, along with source-only backports for the end-of-life 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 branches. The rollout was complicated by a premature public leak, which forced the coordinated disclosure timeline forward.

While the flaws clearly belonged near the top of the patching list, early evidence suggested they were considerably harder to weaponize than initially feared. Successful exploitation requires specific conditions and knowledge of the target, and public proof-of-concept exploits did not work against a default PHP installation, according to Sansec.

On October 22, ESET was among nine security companies that told NBC News they had not seen any successful attacks, even though more than 200 proof-of-concept exploits were circulating. The remediation challenge extends beyond obvious web servers: PHP can also be embedded in appliances, network devices, management interfaces, and third-party products, while end-of-life PHP branches do not receive normal upstream binary releases.

Linux kernel: Reports went public before fixes were ready

As if the PHP issues weren’t severe enough, on October 21, Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent several reports on unpatched Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the kernel’s private security address while also copying public mailing lists. As a result, technical details of vulnerabilities for which fixes were not yet generally available became public, prompting stable kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman to question why the reports had been sent to public lists without patches.

The two most severe issues, both rated CVSS 9.0 by ZDI, affect KSMBD, the Linux kernel’s built-in SMB server. ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in the SMB Direct path that could lead to RCE, while ZDI-CAN-33774 is a race condition that could also lead to RCE. Exploiting ZDI-CAN-33549 requires an RDMA-capable interface, a writable KSMBD share, and SMB Direct negotiation, significantly narrowing the number of systems exposed to that particular attack. Other reports concerned local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the networking stack and the VMware graphics driver, as well as an information disclosure issue in the NVMe target code (NVMET).

To remediate, security teams had to track each report independently, consult distribution advisories, and restrict exposed services where practical while awaiting verified fixes. Kernel updates also required rebooting into the patched kernel and checking the running version, not merely confirming that a new package had been installed.

LiteLLM: Compromised, not merely vulnerable

On October 21, attackers published a malicious version of LiteLLM, 1.107.0, to PyPI and pushed compromised images to the project’s official container registries. According to the project’s incident report, its release pipeline was breached using GitHub CLI credentials associated with three developers. One of the stolen tokens belonged to an owner of the project’s GitHub organization, allowing attackers to disable branch protections and modify the release workflow to point to a lookalike repository. LiteLLM, a Python proxy for LLM providers, has about 23 million weekly downloads, and the malicious version remained available on PyPI for roughly two hours before it was quarantined. It was the project’s second supply-chain compromise of 2026, after malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 appeared in March.

The payload combined a credential stealer with a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT). By abusing Python’s startup mechanisms, including a .pth file, it ran every time Python started, even if an application never imported LiteLLM. Execution therefore did not depend on exploiting an application flaw: simply running Python in an affected environment could be enough.

Affected environments had to be treated as potentially compromised, not merely vulnerable. According to LiteLLM, these included environments that ran litellm==1.107.0 and containers that executed affected images distributed under the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable tags during the compromised intervals. Removing or replacing the package was insufficient: teams needed to determine whether the malicious code had run, contain affected systems, rebuild from clean sources, and rotate exposed secrets from a clean environment. Cloud, source-control, and CI/CD logs also had to be reviewed for unauthorized activity.

Node2Shell: From Node.js to HTTP2Shell

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder, which Node.js bundles. Malformed compressed input can cause crashes, memory disclosure, or potentially RCE when an application decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. This can happen through explicit decompression, compressed request bodies, or automatically decompressed responses. Node.js rates the flaw as high severity, while the broader Brotli vulnerability carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. According to Aikido, researchers demonstrated code execution against the official, unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 image on Linux ARM64. Although the exploit did not work on every attempt, the demonstration showed that exploitation was practical, if not universally reliable.

Node.js shipped fixes on October 21 in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, and Bun followed with version 1.4.4 or later. Node.js 25.x, 23.x, 20.x, and earlier releases are end-of-life and will not receive the fix. Within days, the story outgrew Node.js. The same decoder is compiled into the Python Brotli and brotlicffi packages as well as into other HTTP software, which led researchers to rename the issue HTTP2Shell. The operational challenge was therefore not simply upgrading a single runtime but identifying every container, serverless deployment, and library that bundles the vulnerable decoder. The issue was fixed upstream in Brotli 1.2.1. Notably, OpenAI’s Codex Security had reported the underlying bug, and the fix had been present in the Brotli source since February without being recognized as a security issue.

GitLab: Credential leaks and authorization failures

On October 21, GitLab shipped a critical out-of-band patch release (versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) addressing 12 security vulnerabilities. The headline flaw, CVE-2026-110264, rated 10.0 under CVSS v3.1, is an integer overflow triggered when GitLab compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Under certain conditions, it could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The affected versions date back to GitLab 7.0.

The other fixes addressed credential exposure, cache poisoning, authorization bypasses, and failures to enforce membership or merge-request approval policies. Reported unauthenticated attack paths included exposure of sensitive credentials through internal response headers and manipulation of a shared OAuth/OIDC discovery cache, while other issues required authenticated access. GitLab did not publish individual severity scores or exploitability details for these issues.

GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were already patched, so the work fell on administrators of self-managed instances. GitLab strongly recommended upgrading immediately, but with a catch: the older backport releases (19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13) included only the critical fix, while the remaining 11 issues were fixed only in 19.3.6 and later. Administrators also had to verify that all deployment components had been updated and assess the potential exposure of credentials and private project data due to the fact that patching would not invalidate stolen credentials or reverse unauthorized changes.

eMudhra/emSign: Compromised certificate trust

The high-priority eMudhra/emSign incident involved no software vulnerability at all. Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) had insecure private keys, meaning attackers could potentially create certificates that would be trusted through the affected emSign certificate chain. While browsers had updated their trust stores and revocation lists, some Python tooling continued to trust the compromised intermediate CAs through its own certificate bundles. This created a risk of man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks against TLS connections, including those to python.org and pypi.org.

The Python Software Foundation urged users to upgrade immediately to at least certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, and uv 0.13.4, and the Python core team shipped expedited releases 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16, and 3.11.18 to update the bundled pip. The updates had to reach every host, application, and existing virtual environment. Container images had to be rebuilt with layer caching disabled to fetch the latest system certificates. The decisive check was whether deployed clients rejected the compromised trust paths; simply upgrading Python was not enough.

Cutting through the noise

Cybersecurity Black Week showed that a severity score rarely tells the whole story. A 9.2-rated PHP flaw that attackers struggled to exploit, a 10.0-rated GitLab bug, exposed kernel reports with no patches, and a poisoned package that ran at Python startup each called for a different response. What they all had in common was a window of exposure: the time between disclosure and when the last affected system is patched. For the leaked kernel flaws, that window opened before any fix existed, and for end-of-life PHP versions, it may never fully close. This is where ESET’s multilayered protection comes in, using behavioural detection and other security mechanisms to help block exploitation attempts and keep systems protected until patches are applied.

At the same time, the signals defenders rely on were buried in noise, from scanning that was largely benign to a single behavioural rule firing hundreds of thousands of times in a week. What mattered most was quickly understanding which incidents actually affected an organization's environment and what each incident required. That is the problem ESET’s correlation engine, ESET LiveCortex, and its specialized cybersecurity model, ESET NeoCortex, are designed to solve: turning an overwhelming volume of raw data into understandable incidents so that defenders can act before attackers achieve their goals. To learn how they work, read Beyond the alert: How ESET is teaching AI to understand security incidents.

Title: ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q3 2026
Context: They represent only a subset of the cybersecurity intelligence made available to customers of ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports
Full Text:
ESET APT Activity Report Q2 2026–Q2 2026 summarizes notable activities of selected advanced persistent threat (APT) groups documented by ESET researchers between April and September 2026. The operations presented here reflect the broader threat landscape observed during this period and highlight some of its key trends and developments. They represent only a subset of the cybersecurity intelligence made available to customers of ESET Threat Intelligence APT Reports.

During the monitored period, China-aligned groups conducted intelligence-collection operations primarily against governmental targets. FamousSparrow kept up its monitoring in South America, just as in the previous reporting period. In Southeast Asia and Oceania, China-aligned threat actors ran campaigns that appear to support Chinese law enforcement efforts against organized crime in the region. One threat actor targeted hotels in Palau, which seems to be increasingly used as a base for fraud-related organized crime. SlippyNunchucks deployed its DarkVigil toolset in Sri Lanka against Chinese-speaking individuals connected to fraud schemes, likely in the context of broader regional law enforcement efforts against financial crime. As scam compounds have become an issue for countries neighboring China, with direct negative effects on China itself, it is likely that China-aligned APT groups have supported law enforcement efforts in this area. Another, broader cluster of activity targeted Taiwanese organizations operating in the semiconductor industry. This focus on Taiwan’s semiconductor sector is consistent with long-running Chinese industrial espionage priorities, and the strategic importance of semiconductor supply chains to both economic competition and national security.

Middle East-aligned activity increased compared with the previous reporting period, driven mainly by the return of several established Iran-aligned groups. In the previous period, activity from these groups had declined, most likely because internet restrictions imposed by the Iranian regime hindered their own ability to operate effectively. FilthyFeline, a subgroup of OilRig, and MuddyWater resumed operations after a quieter period, with most activity directed at entities in Israel across multiple sectors; a smaller number of US companies were also affected. FilthyFeline also appears to have taken over activity against a cellular data service provider in Uzbekistan that had previously been compromised by BladedFeline, another OilRig subgroup. In parallel, we analyzed new or updated malware, suggesting renewed development activity within parts of the Iran-aligned ecosystem. We also discovered activity by Arid Viper, a Hamas-affiliated threat actor, against what appears to be the Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates or an affiliated governmental entity. Given the ongoing US-led peace process, as well as the long-standing rivalry between Hamas and the Palestinian Authority, this activity was potentially intended to collect intelligence on the Palestinian Authority’s diplomatic position and internal thinking regarding negotiations to reduce hostilities in the region.

North Korea-aligned threat actors did not deviate significantly from the types of targets seen in previous reporting periods. These include primarily technology and cryptocurrency companies, software developers, and other opportunistic targets. Alongside South Korea, Ukraine has become increasingly prominent among North Korea-aligned targets. This is likely related to growing ties between Russia and North Korea, and North Korea’s increasing involvement in Russia’s war against Ukraine, not only through indirect military support (munitions, etc.) but also through the deployment of North Korean soldiers. Alongside these broader trends, Lazarus resumed targeting of the drone sector, typically using recruitment-themed social engineering to gain initial access. The likely motivation is the increasingly important role that drone systems are playing in the war in Ukraine, where new tactics and capabilities are being tested. Access to such knowledge and manufacturing processes could provide North Korea with valuable know-how for developing its own drone-production capabilities. We also detected ScarCruft targeting an African country, which was probably intended either to maintain oversight of a North Korean worker scheme operating in the country or to monitor Russian activities there. Separately, DeceptiveDevelopment moved from fake job-interview lures to broader software supply-chain compromises, harvesting developer credentials and using that access to inject malicious code into public and private source code repositories.

Russia-aligned activity continued to support its war objectives, targeting governments, the defense sector, and military entities in Europe, with a substantially higher number of targets in Ukraine. Looking more closely at these activities, similarities between Russia-aligned and Belarus-aligned campaigns stand out, further supporting our hypothesis that threat actors aligned with the two countries are becoming operationally closer. Gamaredon’s operations, which are typically numerous, saw a significant decline. We suspect that this could be related to Ukrainian attacks on Crimea, where the group is suspected to operate, a broader restructuring of its operations, or other factors that we continue to assess. Despite this decline in activity, Gamaredon updated its PteroBox file stealer and started using new tools such as PteroPSDoor and Turla’s VBScript Rezzuar. PhantomCaptcha attempted to deploy spyware, which we named PrincessSpy, on Android devices while impersonating Ukrainian entities. We also identified an extensive campaign in Ukraine exploiting MDaemon mail servers, during which the attackers deployed two backdoor malware families, HELLAGE and HELLTAG.

North Korea’s expanding military cooperation with Russia has prompted expectations that North Korea-aligned cyberactivity might be starting to align more closely with Russian objectives in Ukraine. While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia. We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas. Most notably, we identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater, marking a significant development in this threat nexus. According to our telemetry, FrostyNeighbor attacked a manufacturing company in Ukraine that plays an important role in the country’s transportation sector. This marks a notable escalation, as threat actors with a well-established history of destructive cyberoperations in Ukraine have, until now, been Russia-aligned.

Finally, we identified several cases of APT groups using AI and large language models (LLMs) at various stages of their operations. Threat actors used AI primarily to accelerate tasks that would otherwise require painstaking effort, including malware development and the creation of decoy websites. In some cases, this resembled vibe coding: rapid, prompt-driven drafting of code, with human operators adapting and integrating the results into their toolchains. We also discovered phishing lures containing images that were clearly AI-generated. In one notable case, Russia-aligned UAC-0099 inserted a decoy request for instructions on building a nuclear weapon into a script comment, apparently attempting to trigger the safety guardrails of LLM-based security analysis and prevent the inspection of the malicious code that followed.

Despite these developments, we have not noticed AI substantially reshaping the APT landscape over the past six months. While we cannot determine whether some operations may involve a higher degree of AI-driven automation, our telemetry continues to show hands-on-keyboard activity and operations that are not fully automated. Overall, our observations suggest that APT groups are currently using AI much like mainstream software developers: to accelerate software development, automate previously manual tasks, and assist with the analysis of large volumes of data, rather than to conduct fully autonomous malicious operations.

Last week, details emerged about a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a server-side scripting language commonly used in web development. The news prompted security advisories from government agencies and sent website owners scrambling to apply the patches, with some sites even going offline as a precaution. This is because on an unpatched server, an attacker can exploit the vulnerabilities to run their own code without logging in. As three out of four websites globally are estimated to use PHP in some capacity, its ubiquity helps create an environment ripe for abuse; indeed, initial attempts to exploit the flaws – discovered by AI and dubbed PHP2Shell – weren't long in coming.

Here's what to know about CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, as well as what website owners and IT teams should do to stay safe – all in a little more than two minutes.

Title: MythicRatatoskr: An Yggdrasil-enabled backdoor deployed in a UAC-0099-Sandworm collaboration
Context: In the past, Gamaredon collaborated with a threat actor that we discovered and named InvisiMole
Full Text:
Executive summary

This report analyzes activity during which UAC‑0099 gained initial access on July 16th, 2025 and handed it off to Sandworm, which then conducted a data-wiping attack on September 17th, 2025. It particularly focuses on the MythicRatatoskr backdoor, which is unique in its use of the Yggdrasil mesh network to communicate with a C&C server hosted within it.

We presented our findings about MythicRatatoskr at LABScon on September 18th, 2026, and at the Virus Bulletin conference on October 16th, 2026.

Key points of this blogpost:

On July 16th, 2025, UAC-0099 gained initial access to a grain logistics company in Ukraine via a spearphishing email with a malicious attachment, leading to the execution chain of the MATCHWOK backdoor.

One day later, the attackers deployed MythicRatatoskr, a previously undocumented backdoor that communicates with a C&C server hosted inside the Yggdrasil mesh network. We have not seen the backdoor used anywhere else, and we found indications that a Linux variant may also exist.

Yggdrasil is a decentralized mesh network that implements an experimental routing scheme in which the IPv6 communication between the nodes is end-to-end protected.

Ultimately, UAC-0099 handed off access to Sandworm, which then carried out a data-wiping attack.

Cooperation among Russia-aligned actors

The handover documented in this report is not an isolated phenomenon. As noted above, Sandworm is attributed to GRU Unit 74455, and UAC-0099’s targeting leads us to assess that it is aligned with Russian interests.

Earlier in 2025, we uncovered that Russia-aligned Gamaredon collaborated with Turla, another Russia-aligned threat actor; we documented our findings in our blogpost Gamaredon X Turla collab. Both groups are linked to the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation (FSB). This kind of cooperation underscores the potential for coordinated cyberespionage campaigns among Russia-aligned groups, likely intended to amplify their operational impact. In the past, Gamaredon collaborated with a threat actor that we discovered and named InvisiMole. Against that backdrop, a UAC‑0099-to-Sandworm handoff is unusual in the specific actors involved, but no longer surprising as a pattern.

Overview of the intrusion

According to ESET telemetry, the events unfolded as follows: at 06:59 on July 16th, 2025, a scheduled task named pdfopentask was executed on one machine in the target organization. It executed a PowerShell payload from %temp%\temporarydoc.txt.

A minute later, MATCHBOIL was deployed. MATCHBOIL is a downloader that deployed, in this case, the MATCHWOK backdoor (C&C: https://uztickets[.]com) from https://egyptanimals[.]com/animals/photoalbum. The following day, at 09:28, a new binary was delivered to the machine: the MythicRatatoskr backdoor. Due to the close proximity of time, we believe with high confidence that the MATCHWOK execution chain led to the deployment of MythicRatatoskr. Our telemetry further shows that additional MythicRatatoskr samples were subsequently deployed to other machines within the organization, this time using an OpenSSH SFTP server.

Later, ESET telemetry detected a SOCKS5 server on some of the machines, with one sample having been extracted from an unknown archive using WinRAR. We believe that the SOCKS5 server was deployed using MythicRatatoskr.

Approximately two months later, on September 17th, 2025, we detected data-wiping activity at the compromised grain logistics company. The data-wiping attack was executed by deploying the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy – standard Sandworm tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that we have observed numerous times in ESET telemetry.

Therefore, we assess that UAC‑0099 can act as an initial access group for Sandworm.

This blogpost focuses primarily on the analysis of the MythicRatatoskr backdoor, the Yggdrasil network that hosts its C&C server, and the accompanying SOCKS5 server. The first versions of MATCHBOIL and MATCHWOK have already been analyzed by CERT‑UA in its advisory, with MATCHBOIL and its evolution further covered in our blogpost MATCHBOIL: New tricks, same old evil intentions. These tools are therefore omitted here.

A squirrel in the world tree

The word Yggdrasil originates in Norse mythology, where it refers to a sacred tree connecting the various realms of the cosmos. Within that tree lives a squirrel named Ratatoskr that carries messages between its top and its roots. Given the backdoor’s role as a messenger scurrying through the Yggdrasil network, we decided to name the backdoor MythicRatatoskr.

More technically, Yggdrasil is a decentralized mesh network that connects devices directly to each other without a central hub, building an encrypted IPv6 overlay on top of the internet so that participating nodes can exchange end-to-end-protected traffic. Legitimate users adopt such meshes for resilient connectivity, research, and hobby networking. Because no single server runs the mesh, the network is robust and hard to disrupt – properties that also make it attractive to adversaries. Importantly, Yggdrasil is not designed to provide anonymity.

Attribution

The post-compromise execution chain relied on known malware already attributed to UAC‑0099 – namely the MATCHBOIL downloader and the MATCHWOK backdoor – which leads us to attribute this stage of the attack to UAC‑0099 with high confidence. We attribute the data-wiping activity observed two months later to Sandworm, also with high confidence, based on the TTPs involved.

Moreover, we assess with high confidence that UAC‑0099 handed off access to Sandworm at some point during the intrusion, although we have not yet been able to determine whether the MythicRatatoskr backdoor was operated primarily by UAC‑0099 or by Sandworm.

UAC‑0099 profile

UAC‑0099 is a cyberespionage group targeting governmental organizations, financial institutions, and media, all in Ukraine. Based on the targeting, we believe with medium confidence that the group is aligned with Russian interests. UAC‑0099 can act as an initial access broker for Sandworm, a Russia-aligned group best known for its destructive attacks in Ukraine.

The group has been active since at least 2022 and was first reported by CERT‑UA in June 2023. Apart from MATCHBOIL, the group also typically deploys LONEPAGE, a PowerShell downloader named after the presence of the word page in its C&C URLs.

Sandworm profile

Sandworm is a Russia-aligned threat group that performs destructive attacks. It is mostly known for attacks against Ukrainian energy companies in December 2015 and December 2016, which resulted in power outages. In June 2017 Sandworm launched the NotPetya data-wiping attack that used a supply-chain vector by compromising the Ukrainian accounting software M.E.Doc. In February 2018, Sandworm launched the Olympic Destroyer data-wiping attack against organizers of the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang.

The Sandworm group uses such advanced malware as Industroyer, which is able to communicate with equipment at energy companies via industrial control protocols. In April 2022, CERT‑UA thwarted an attack against an energy company in Ukraine where the Sandworm group tried to deploy a new variant of this malware, Industroyer2.

Since February 2022, Sandworm has been very active in Ukraine, by deploying data wipers against strategic organizations.

In October 2020, the US Department of Justice published an indictment against six Russian computer hackers that it alleges prepared and conducted various Sandworm attacks. As we already mentioned, the group is commonly attributed to GRU’s Unit 74455.

Compromise chain

Initial access and execution

According to ESET telemetry, initial access was gained via a spearphishing email with a malicious attachment – a finding that matches CERT‑UA blogpost. We assess that the MATCHWOK backdoor execution chain (already documented in the CERT‑UA blogpost) then led to the execution of MythicRatatoskr, a backdoor that communicates with its C&C server over the Yggdrasil network. Subsequently, the attackers probably used MythicRatatoskr to deliver a SOCKS5 server.

Persistence

MATCHBOIL persists MATCHWOK by adding the registry value UpdateMonitor to the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\, with data pointing to the dropped MATCHWOK path.

MythicRatatoskr is started as a Windows service with the name ieupdate.

Collection and exfiltration

During check-in, MythicRatatoskr sends information about the current user, hostname, and local network settings to the C&C server. In addition, the operators can use MythicRatatoskr to exfiltrate files and screenshots to the C&C server by using HTTPS routed through the Yggdrasil mesh network. The data is not staged prior to exfiltration.

Toolset

MythicRatatoskr

MythicRatatoskr is a backdoor written in Go that uses the Yggdrasil network (described in the Network protocol section) to reach its C&C server. As noted earlier, we named the backdoor after Ratatoskr, the squirrel from Norse mythology that scurries through Yggdrasil – the sacred tree connecting the realms of the cosmos – carrying messages between its top and its roots. We felt this was a fitting parallel for a backdoor that ferries data across the Yggdrasil network. There are signs in the binaries suggesting that the development started sometime between December 2024 and February 2025.

Function names left in the binaries – following a mix of mixed caps (CheckInAgent) and snake case (agent_run) – suggest either code merged from another project or inconsistent naming by the authors. Key functions handle service registration and Yggdrasil network initialization (main, runService), check-in and beaconing (agent_run, init_agent, CheckInAgent), configuration handling (saveConfig, Encrypt, Decrypt), command polling and dispatch (getTasks, doTask), and the backdoor commands themselves (upload, download, screencat, shell, manageProxy, etc.).

Some samples also include a 10-minute startup delay, likely to avoid immediately connecting to the Yggdrasil network on execution, helping to evade detection.

Persistence

Network protocol

To communicate with the C&C server, MythicRatatoskr relies on the Yggdrasil network – a decentralized mesh network in an alpha state that implements an experimental routing scheme. Each node in the network generates its own Ed25519 key pair, which allows protected end-to-end IPv6 communication between the peers. The IPv6 address is derived from the public key in the 200::/7 subnet range, which was deprecated by IETF in 2004. Anonymity is not among the goals of the project. We explore this topic more in the Network infrastructure section.

The yggdrasil-go repository already provides the necessary types and methods to join the Yggdrasil network. There’s also another project, called yggstack, that enables the Yggdrasil network to communicate via a network stack in the user space. This has the benefit of not needing to create a tunnel interface, which might be an issue if the user does not have the required privileges to create one, or if such an interface is not supported on the system. The MythicRatatoskr code is based on yggstack, making the malware portable.

There’s a publicly available network that one can join by adding at least one public peer into the Yggdrasil configuration. MythicRatatoskr specifically contains an embedded base64-encoded blob that contains a list of public peers in the URI format. Most peers on the list are still operational. MythicRatatoskr randomly picks three peers from the hardcoded list, which is the recommended number, and connects to them in order to join this public Yggdrasil network.

Once MythicRatatoskr is part of the Yggdrasil network, it communicates with its C&C server, which is also part of the network, via HTTPS on port 443.

Communication uses JSON-encoded HTTP POST requests containing a uuid (explained in Table 4, in the MythicRatatoskr main configuration section), a message type, and optional data. Four message types exist:

checkin – register the backdoor and send victim metadata such as username, hostname, and local IPs; the server responds with a fresh uuid and psk),

tasking – poll for new commands,

result – return command output, base64-encoded when present,

and getfile – retrieve file content for the upload command.

Although the C&C server is hosted in the Yggdrasil network – which may prevent network security tools from detecting outbound connections to it – blocking the public peer addresses is a viable mitigation.

Configuration

We distinguish between two types of configuration:

a backdoor-specific configuration used by the malware itself; and

an Yggdrasil configuration used to join the mesh network.

MythicRatatoskr main configuration

The MythicRatatoskr configuration is stored in a file at a hardcoded path. The path can differ in each sample; we identified the following paths:

C:\Windows\Temp\.updatecache (in krbtman.exe, Act64.exe, ie.exe, ieupdate.exe, and windowsdefendersvc.exe)

C:\Windows\system32\.updatecache (in updater.exe, and windowsdefendersvc.exe)

%LocalAppData%/Temp/.crond (only in OneDriveLiveUpdater.exe)

The %LocalAppData%/Temp/.crond path is notable, since such a filename (.crond) along with forward slashes is expected for Unix-like systems. This indicates that a Linux variant (or macOS, FreeBSD, etc., though less likely) of MythicRatatoskr may also exist. Moreover, OneDriveLiveUpdater.exe contains an unused configuration path /tmp/.test_config; the filename suggests that this configuration path may have been used during testing and accidentally left in a Windows deployment.

All of the configuration filenames start with a dot. On Unix-like systems, programs used for listing files, such as ls, typically exclude these entries by default, effectively hiding them. This is not the case on Windows, where these files are not hidden. This further suggests the existence of a Linux variant.

The backdoor-specific configuration stored on disk is a JSON file encrypted via AES‑256‑CFB using a hardcoded key embedded in the binary, US3pM9KFxrZBSgc1pGl2wO4Kir1XjZP5Z9kBXBMYd2s=, which is decoded using base64 before being used. The first 16 bytes of the file represent the IV.

The configuration file is not required for the malware to start. MythicRatatoskr contains an embedded default configuration, which it encrypts and writes to disk during initialization. This allows operators to deploy the malware without a separate configuration file and update the configuration later via C&C commands. Backdoor commands are described later in the Capabilities section.

Yggdrasil configuration

Initially, when MythicRatatoskr starts, it generates a new Yggdrasil configuration, including a new Ed25519 private key. Because the Yggdrasil IPv6 address is derived from the public key, the victim machine’s Yggdrasil IPv6 address changes each time the malware runs.

MythicRatatoskr then uses empty NodeInfo data and sets the NodeInfoPrivacy flag. As a result, other nodes in the Yggdrasil network won’t be able to get more information about the node, such as the Yggdrasil version or the operating system on which the node is running.

The backdoor uses a publicly available Yggdrasil network to reach the C&C server. To join the network, it needs to connect to at least one of the publicly available peers. All MythicRatatoskr samples contain the same embedded list of 32 peers from which three are randomly picked. The peer list is base64 encoded in the binary and was likely compiled by the backdoor authors from publicly available sources. We provide the full peer list at the end of the blogpost.

Capabilities

MythicRatatoskr supports standard backdoor functionality, including command execution, file system navigation, file transfer, screenshot capture, and proxying. Table 3 contains all of the backdoor commands; the command IDs are strings that are hardcoded in the code.

Most of the code was copied from existing open-source projects, such as revsocks, as implied by the presence of debug strings like Accepting stream and Passing off to socks5, and the function name connectForSocks.

Unlike the standalone SOCKS5 server described below, MythicRatatoskr’s proxy command is used to create a reverse SOCKS5 proxy connection. The standalone tool creates a local SOCKS5 server instead.

SOCKS5 server

The SOCKS5 server exclusively used by UAC‑0099 or Sandworm during the August 2025 activity is a simple tool written in Go that uses go-socks5 for managing proxy connections. The tool is internally named bindProxy.

Because MythicRatatoskr already includes SOCKS5 proxy functionality (see Table 3), it is unclear why the attackers deployed a separate SOCKS5 server. It is possible that MythicRatatoskr’s proxy command did not work as expected, so the operators installed this additional tool. Nevertheless, together they support both forward and reverse proxying.

Capabilities

The tool uses go-socks5 to create a SOCKS5 proxy server that listens on 127.0.0.1, port 33690. The address is specifically used to allow only the local machine to access the service. To make the proxy server reachable from outside the victim’s network, the attackers could have used MythicRatatoskr’s expose command to expose it through the Yggdrasil network. Alternatively, they may have used another existing tunnel to access the machine.

Network infrastructure

As stated in its FAQ, Yggdrasil is not anonymous, so it is possible to locate nodes in the Yggdrasil network. First, we tried to find the C&C server 201:b479:2771:8df4:b5eb:d007:63b0[:]2838, which we extracted from the MythicRatatoskr configuration, in the publicly available map of the Yggdrasil network at http://51.15.204.214/ to no avail because the map was last updated on August 8th, 2024, nearly a year before the intrusion took place.

We therefore generated our own map of the network’s spanning tree, which does include the C&C server, as shown in Figure 1. The C&C server is situated near the center of the tree, making it easily reachable from other peers. The colors of each node indicate how far the node is from the C&C server. For example, as indicated by the red color, the connection from/to the nodes at the edge can be unreliable. The coordinates (Coords) for the C&C are rather simple: the server is reachable via the node with ID 4, which is the root of the spanning tree.

Using Yggdrasil’s command line utility yggdrasilctl, we identified that the C&C server is configured with three public peers, shown in Figure 2.

The C&C server’s port 443 uses TLS certificates that are rotated regularly. This pattern is characteristic of certificates generated by revsocks, on which the server code is probably based.

Conclusion

In this campaign, we observed cooperation, or at least operational handoff, between two Russia-aligned threat groups with different roles. UAC‑0099 appears to have gained initial access to a Ukrainian logistics company using its known tooling. That access was later used in activity culminating in a destructive Sandworm operation.

In addition, we identified a new backdoor, MythicRatatoskr, which is attributed to either UAC‑0099 or Sandworm. The C&C server for this backdoor is hosted within the Yggdrasil mesh network, and the use of such infrastructure made determining the server’s physical location particularly challenging. The backdoor was probably used to deploy the SOCKS5 server to route connections through the compromised network.

To our knowledge, this is the first documented case of Yggdrasil being abused in this way by a state-aligned threat actor, and it may signal a broader trend of adversaries adopting experimental peer-to-peer networks to increase the resilience and stealth of their infrastructure.

Ultimately, Sandworm carried out a data-wiping attack by deploying the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy, a technique consistent with previous Sandworm destructive operations.

Title: Is the ad a scam? How to tell before you click
Context: Also known as malvertising, a click on this kind of ad will exploit browser/software vulnerabilities or trick you into unwittingly installing malware via an app download
Full Text:
Fraudulent ads have been around for about as long as the advertising industry. Today, they often reach you through social media feeds, apps and search results you use every day, and the platforms showing them can also (inadvertently) help build them. In September, the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) asked whether platforms should be required to stop impersonation scam ads from ever reaching consumers. Its concern is the ad tools that those platforms offer to advertisers. They can generate the copy, images and video, and optimize who sees the result, regardless of whether the ads are legitimate or not.

In Europe, nearly one trillion scam ads were served to social media users in 2025, generating an estimated £3.8 billion in revenue for these platforms. In the US, data is harder to come by, although Meta alone projected 10% of its 2024 revenue would come from ads for scams and banned goods, amounting to a staggering $16 billion.

For consumers, the message is clear: you might trust the platform, but you can’t trust the ads on it.

What do scam ads look like?

Scam ads could appear on search engine pages, e-commerce marketplaces and shopping sites, mobile apps and games, video sites, messaging platforms and a host of other websites. But perhaps the biggest risk comes from social media sites. Nearly a third (30%) of people who reported losing money to a scam last year said it started on social media.

They could include advertising that:

Impersonates a legitimate company and leads to a phishing site designed to mimic the real version

Offers special deals on goods for a limited time, as a way to create a sense of urgency

Offers investment opportunities, often in cryptocurrency ventures, that promise high returns with no downside

Impersonates customer support for legitimate companies like banks

Promises mega giveaways of cash and prizes which only require the user to share personal and financial information to access

Scares the victim with fake security warnings that their computer or device is infected

Engages the victim with clickbait such as outrageous news stories with sensational headlines

What’s the end goal?

These ads serve various purposes. Some may be outright malicious. Also known as malvertising, a click on this kind of ad will exploit browser/software vulnerabilities or trick you into unwittingly installing malware via an app download. Others are designed to persuade you into handing over personal information via prize giveaways, questionnaires and other phishing-style pages. This could subsequently be used to commit identity fraud.

Another category of scam ads will target your finances more directly. They may ask for money to invest in a fictitious scheme, pay for a non-existent product, or hand over money to pay a fake fee, for example. In some cases, the scam ad may take you to a fake e-commerce site which covertly harvests your card details.

While these efforts are often digital, beware too of calling phone numbers on ads. They might put you through to a scam call center where the operatives will be trained to relieve you of your money and/or personal/financial information. This is often what happens if you get swindled by a fake security alert.

Banks hate these scams because, in jurisdictions like the UK, they are responsible for reimbursing customers for “authorized push payment” (APP) losses in some instances. They have long argued that social media platforms in particular should do more to police this content, and to compensate victims. However, in the US and elsewhere, social media companies aren’t legally bound to do so, despite profiting from the ad revenue.

This may change, of course, depending on the outcome of the FTC’s rulemaking, which is at its earliest stage. It says it may consider forcing platforms to vet advertisers, monitor posted ads, investigate scams, remove fraudulent advertising, and pursue disciplinary action, among other measures.

Scam-ad red flags: what to look out for

In the meantime, the best you can do is to spot the warning signs of a scam and steer well clear of suspect ads. You should be able to spot them by looking out for a few common red flags that include:

Urgent language encouraging you to act quickly. This rushes us into making decisions that otherwise we may not make, like sharing our personal information.

Too-good-to-be-true offers that trigger our fear of missing out. These are often presented as time-sensitive in order to ramp up the urgency.

Any requests for sensitive personal information, which could help fraudsters build a profile of us with which to use for identity fraud. It could be details as innocuous as email/home address, phone number and full name.

Phone numbers on ads that will probably route you to a scam call center. Most legitimate companies funnel support issues through digital channels initially.

Pressure to download software in order to fix an ‘issue’ with your computer/device.

Sensational news designed to tantalize and persuade you to click through.

Celebrity endorsements for products and services for sale (sometimes deepfaked), or investment opportunities.

What happens if I’ve fallen victim to a scam ad?

If you’ve clicked through on a scam ad or called the number, and then downloaded something, handed over some personal/financial information, used your card to buy something, or made a bank transfer, don’t panic. Also:

Don’t reply to any further messages from the scammer and monitor your accounts for suspicious activity.

If relevant, contact your bank or card provider immediately and tell them what happened. They should be able to freeze your card or account while they investigate. If you’ve made a transfer, it will fall under an APP fraud claim. Card payments may be eligible for a chargeback.

If you’ve handed over passwords, change them immediately on the relevant site and anywhere else you’ve reused them. Switch on two-factor authentication (2FA) for these sites and consider using a password manager to store strong, unique credentials for every account.

If you’ve downloaded anything, run a scan using security software from a reputable provider. And ensure your operating system and all applications are all up to date.

Preserve evidence of the scam where possible. This includes the ad itself, and any URLs, screenshots, emails/messages, payment records or correspondence with the scammer. It will help if you’re able to proceed with a reimbursement claim.

Report the ad to the platform that showed it, using its built-in reporting option, and report the scam to the authorities, e.g. the FTC (US) or Report Fraud (UK).

Scam ads are getting easier to generate thanks to AI, and can look increasingly professional, even including video content. That puts more pressure on you to spot the warning signs. Stay safe.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

Why are there so many scam ads on Facebook and Instagram?

Scammers place them there to get maximum exposure, knowing the platforms don’t police their content rigorously. They may want your personal/financial information, or to trick you into buying a non-existent product. They may even want to con you into a fake investment.

How can I tell if an ad is a scam?

It might use urgent language and too-good-to-be-true offers, potentially endorsed by celebrities. It may ask for sensitive personal information, or feature phone numbers that take you to a call center where operatives will ask for the same details or urge you to download remote access software. It might claim your PC is infected with malware and pressure you into taking action. It could even deliver sensational news designed to encourage click throughs.

Can I get my money back if I paid through a scam ad?

Social media companies are not required by law to compensate users that may have been defrauded. But depending on where you live you may be able to file an APP claim with your bank. If you’ve made a card payment, you may be able to file a chargeback claim.

What should I do if I’ve fallen victim to a scam ad?

Don’t panic. Preserve the evidence and stop any communication with the scammer. Monitor your accounts for suspicious activity. Change any passwords you’ve shared and switch on 2FA. Contact your bank or card provider, tell them what happened, and ask them to freeze your bank account/card. If you’ve downloaded anything, run a security scan and ensure your operating system and software are all up to date. Report the ad to the platform and the scam to the authorities.
