Title: Inbox flooded with sign-up messages? Email bombing explained
Context: First, an attacker gets hold of your email address
Full Text:
In September, reports emerged that a Virginia woman had been submerged by a flood of emails. Hundreds of automated messages poured in over a 24-hour period, including newsletters and promotions she’d never signed up to. But this was no ordinary spam campaign. The real reason behind the inbox blitz was to bury a legitimate email from the victim’s bank warning her about a fraudulent laptop purchase.

This is email bombing. And if it’s happened to you, it could be a warning sign that your identity or online accounts have been hijacked by fraudsters.

What is email bombing?

Sometimes called “form bombing,” “list bombing” or “subscription bombing,” email bombing attacks usually follow the same pattern. First, an attacker gets hold of your email address. They could do this from historic data breaches, marketing databases, online leaks, or even a prior phishing attack. Once they have it, they’ll use automated, bot-powered tools to sign up for hundreds or thousands of legitimate online services like newsletters, subscriptions, mailing lists, free trials, and competitions.

These will each generate a welcome email or similar. And because they are usually legitimate services, they’re often not blocked by spam filters. The result is an inbox overflowing with messages.

Why do they do it? Two reasons are behind most email bombing attempts:

The scammer is trying to distract the victim so that they don’t see a genuine email among all of the artificially generated ones. They may have hijacked one of your accounts and reset the password, triggering a notification to your inbox. Or they may have made a fraudulent purchase in your name, with the invoice subsequently emailed to you. The main point is to create a smokescreen which prevents you from tackling the more serious fraud.

The hacker may subsequently contact you pretending to be a tech support engineer. They’ll claim to be able to solve your email ‘problem’ and either request a fee to do so, or trick you into installing remote access software so they can take a look at your machine. That could enable them to steal sensitive information on your computer like passwords stored in the browser. Or even install additional malware.

In a corporate scenario, the bomber is most likely trying to distract the cybersecurity team from a more serious attack, such as a data breach or a business email compromise or invoice fraud attempt. Alternatively, they may be trying to disrupt operations as leverage for extortion – ransomware affiliates have used email bombing as a precursor to a fake IT help desk contact in order to get remote access. Or it could even be a disgruntled employee or former worker.

I’ve been email bombed: what next?

If you’ve logged on to find your inbox overwhelmed, don’t panic. Rather than try to unsubscribe to all of the random services you’ve been signed up to, focus your energy on finding the threat that your attacker wanted to hide. Search for security alerts, new device sign-ins, email/phone number changes, password changes/resets, or purchases. Look through your spam folder as well as your inbox, in case the message has ended up there.

If you don’t immediately see anything out of the blue, check your most sensitive accounts individually. These could include

Bank/PayPal/credit card/crypto

Apple/Google/Microsoft

Social media accounts

Look for any suspicious activity: new devices or payment methods added, passwords that may have been changed, and/or recovery details altered. It’s also worth checking your email forwarding rules and sent/deleted items folders for anything unusual.

If you notice something unusual, try to lock the hacker out by changing the password to a unique, strong credential, and enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for extra login security. Ensure the correct recovery email address/phone number is listed (or they may be able to reset the account again). Contact the company itself if you’re concerned about fraud.

Remember to preserve anything related to a possible account takeover or fraud attempt. Only purge when you’re confident it’s over. You can do this more quickly by trying to identify patterns in the messages (e.g., senders, date ranges, domains, etc.). Then you can bulk select and delete in batches.

It goes without saying that you should put the phone down immediately if anyone calls you claiming to be a tech expert who can sort out your email problem.

How to prevent email bombing

Of course, prevention is usually better than cure. And while it’s not always possible to stop your email ending up in the wrong hands, you can limit the damage by ensuring that it’s not exposed on public-facing web pages like social media profiles. Also follow security best practices to stay safe from phishing attacks.

Next, keep your most sensitive accounts as secure as possible. This includes your primary email address, which will be used to receive password reset messages from other online accounts. Use a password manager to ensure they all have strong, unique credentials. And 2FA for an extra layer of security (e.g., via an authenticator app or passkey).

It may also be worth using a secondary email address for less important correspondence like shopping, travel and other leisure activities. This way, if this account is hit by an email bomb, at least your most important messages (bank, government, healthcare etc) are safe.

There’s no silver bullet to prevent email bombing. But account security best practices will help to reduce the chances of an explosion of messages in your inbox.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

Why is my inbox full of hundreds of sign-up emails?

You may be the victim of an email bomb (aka form bomb/list bomb/subscription bomb). A fraudster has used automated tools to sign your email address up to new services for one of two reasons. Either they’re hoping to bury a legitimate security or anti-fraud message, or they’re going to call you pretending to be a tech support engineer that can help.

Has my email account been hacked if it’s full of sign-up emails?

Probably not. Fraudsters may have scraped it off the public web, harvested it from a historic data breach, or even bought it from a marketing database. However, the security/fraud ‘event’ they’re trying to hide with the email bomb tactic may have involved account takeover.

My inbox is full of new messages; what should I do?

First, search for the notification they’re trying to hide in the spam and preserve it. Search for security alerts, new device sign-ins, email/phone number changes, password changes/resets, or purchases. Look through your spam folder as well as your inbox. If you don’t find the message, check your sensitive accounts (bank, social media, tech etc) for unusual activity. Change passwords to a unique, strong credential, and add enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for extra log-in security.

I’ve been email bombed. Should I unsubscribe to all of the new emails?

No, it’s important to find the security notification or fraud warning the attacker is trying to hide, and preserve it. Only purge once you’re confident the issue has been resolved. Consider speeding up the process by deleting in batches (search for common senders, date ranges, domains etc.).

What if someone contacts me to fix the problem?

They’re a fraudster who wants to charge you a fee or trick you into installing remote access software on your machine, which could lead to malware or data theft. Put the phone down on them.

Title: Medicare scam calls, texts and ads: What to watch for this Open Enrollment
Context: And with Medicare Open Enrollment, they have a perfect opportunity to exploit victim expectations, masking their fraud under the cover of legitimate activity
Full Text:
Scammers love a pretext. And with Medicare Open Enrollment, they have a perfect opportunity to exploit victim expectations, masking their fraud under the cover of legitimate activity. From October 15 to December 7 beneficiaries are able to review and amend various parts of their plan. There’ll be ads, emails, messages and calls from genuine insurers at this time. Some might even ask for personal and health details.

That provides great cover for fraudsters, and enough plausibility for even skeptical consumers to drop their guard. Here’s what to look out for.

How do these Medicare scams work?

There are various ways scammers could approach you. They could call, message, email, or send a note on social media. They might also place an ad on Google, mocking up a website with official-looking logos and language to appear as if it’s a legitimate insurer, a specialist agency, or even Medicare itself.

The pretext for getting in touch, or posting the ad, could vary. Common ones include:

You should compare/change your plan by the December 7 deadline

Your Medicare card needs updating or replacing

You could qualify for additional benefits or lower premiums

Your existing coverage (or specific prescription coverage) is changing

You could be eligible for a new plan

They need to verify your account details

Your account has been linked to fraudulent activity

All seem plausible. But the scammer will usually employ some tried-and-tested social engineering techniques to pull you into their deceit. Urgency is a common tactic. It fires our synapses in specific ways that make us stressed and less likely to think logically, while possibly also triggering a fear of missing out. The real deadline of December 7 adds an element of truth to the lie that makes it more plausible still.

If you were told by an official-sounding representative that you could lose your benefits if you don’t act, or that you have just days to claim a lower premium offer, would you stop and think?

If they’re successful, the scammer will move on to the next stage: harvesting your personal, financial and/or medical information. They might ask for your:

Medicare number

Social Security number

Date of birth

Phone number

Email and home address

Account passwords

Health information such as doctors, prescriptions and medical records

Insurance information including provider, plan, member ID and policy details

Bank details and/or credit card information

Once you’ve handed some or all of the above over, you’re unlikely to ever hear from the scammers again. But in the background, they’ll be working hard to monetize your information for their own gain.

What do they want with your data?

There are various ways they might do this, depending on what data they’ve tricked you into handing over. They might want to commit various forms of identity fraud, using your personal and financial details to access your bank and personal accounts, or take out new credit lines in your name.

Alternatively, they may try to use your information to submit fraudulent Medicare claims in your name, for services, equipment or prescriptions that you never received. Or to actually obtain these goods and services. Scammers might even try to manipulate your Medicare enrollment in order to generate fraudulent commissions or compensation.

In September 2026, the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) identified around $17.5 billion in suspicious financial activity that may be linked to healthcare fraud like this.

Depending on exactly what avenue the scammers explore, an incident could leave you out of pocket, impact your coverage, impair your medical records, and plunge you into a bureaucratic nightmare that leaves you in severe emotional and mental distress.

How to spot and avoid Medicare scams

All of which makes it more important than ever that you’re able to spot the tell-tale signs of a Medicare scam at this time of year. You should be extremely dubious of any unsolicited contact, especially if the individual asks for personal, financial or health details. And even more so if they try to pressure you into handing over this information, or promise benefits that seem too good to be true.

Yes, genuine insurers might get in touch seemingly out of the blue. But this will usually not be without your prior consent. And they should never try to strong-arm you into handing over details.

The best approach to steering clear of Medicare scams during Open Enrollment season is to:

Spot the warning signs listed above, and if in doubt, put down the phone or don’t reply to the message. You can always verify separately with the caller/sender to check if they are legitimate (using contact details sourced separately from the inbound contact).

Be very careful about online searches. Don’t click through on any Google ads, and if you’re looking for official Medicare sites be sure the address has a .gov ending.

Type the name of the site you want to visit directly into the search/address bar. Medicare is at Medicare.gov (800-633-4227), while HealthCare.gov (800-318-2596) is where to check if you qualify for savings. Help is also available from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), or local Senior Medicare Patrol.

Report any suspicious contact.

What a real call looks like

Some insurers and other third parties may pick up the phone to get in touch during the Open Enrollment period. But you should be able to tell them apart from fraudsters because they will clearly identify themselves and their organization and give a detailed explanation of why they’re calling. They won’t use pressure tactics or offer too-goo-to-be-true gifts and benefits. And they won’t try to force you to hand over sensitive information straight off the bat.

They should be courteous and provide you with ways to verify who they say they are, even if it means hanging up. And they’ll often be calling because you initiated contact with their organization.

What to do if you’ve already been scammed

If you feel like you’ve fallen victim to a Medicare scammer, don’t panic. Work through the following steps:

Call or contact Medicare at Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227 to report the incident. Also tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general

If you have handed over your bank account/card details, contact your bank and check if you can freeze your card

If you’ve handed over other identity-related information, consider reporting the incident to IdentityTheft.gov

Check your Medicare claims and records for any unusual activity or charges

Contact your healthcare provider/insurer if you have seen any fraudulent activity

Change any passwords you might have handed over to the scammers, across any sites you reuse them on

Don’t fall for recovery fraud. If anyone gets in touch after an incident promising to get your money back or sort everything out on your account for a fee, it’s another scam

Your health is important. But so is your personal information. So slow down this Open Enrollment season and verify every request for personal and medical details.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

When is Medicare Open Enrollment?

It runs from October 15 to December 7 each year, during which time you can make some changes to your coverage.

Would Medicare or my insurer ever call me during Open Enrollment?

A representative from Medicare, your insurer or a third party may call. But put the phone down if they start pressuring you into handing over your details, asking for financial information, or promising too-good-to-be-true benefits. Call them directly to double check, eg 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

What are the main red flags for a Medicare scam?

Watch out for unsolicited contact, especially if the individual asks for personal, financial or health details. And even more so if they try to pressure you into handing over this information, or promise benefits that seem too good to be true. Contact could come via email, phone, social media, or text. Scammers might also buy Google ads to lure you.

What do Medicare scammers want?

They want your medical, financial, personal and possibly your insurance details. They might want this to commit identity fraud, access your bank account, submit fraudulent Medicare claims or obtain goods and services in your name, or manipulate your enrollment.

Can a Medicare scam affect my healthcare?

Yes. Fraudulent claims or misuse of your medical identity could impact your insurance coverage, medical records, prescriptions and access to healthcare. It may also land you with plenty of distressing administrative work to clear your name.

How do I know if a phone call is a Medicare scam or not?

They should clearly identify themselves and their organization and give a detailed explanation of why they’re calling. They won’t use pressure tactics or offer too-goo-to-be-true gifts and benefits. And they won’t try to force you to hand over sensitive information straightaway. They should allow you to hang up and verify their identity. Usually they’ll only call because you have requested it.

What should I do after falling for a Medicare scam?

Call or contact Medicare at Medicare.gov or 800-633-4227 to report the incident. Also tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general. If you’ve handed over your bank account/card details, contact your bank and check if you can freeze your card. Check your Medicare claims and records for any unusual activity or charges. Contact your healthcare provider/insurer if you have seen any fraudulent activity. Change any passwords you might have handed over to the scammers, across any sites you reuse them on. Don’t fall for recovery fraud scammers who promise to get your money back.

Title: What to do when a data breach notice doesn't say much
Context: And if there’s a chance that broader disclosure could help other threat actors (by revealing the attack path and defensive weaknesses) or the adversary itself (if it is still...
Full Text:
Publicly reported data breaches hit an all-time high in the US last year, with over 3,300 incidents recorded and nearly 280 million victim notices mailed out. But are all of these worth the paper they’re written on? Increasingly, they lack crucial details.

As the volume of data breach incidents increases, there’s a growing chance that you’ll be caught up in one. According to the non-profit Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC), over 471 million victim notices went out in the first half of 2026 alone. Yet just a quarter (24%) contained details about the attack vector. That’s the lowest ever rate recorded by the ITRC.

This is bad news for consumers, corporate victims and policymakers. A lack of detail prevents you from understanding your true risk exposure or taking meaningful action to limit the fallout and possibly prevent it from happening again. ITRC’s own data shows that three-quarters of victims want a plain-language list of exactly what data was compromised.

Why are organizations cagey about releasing details?

There are many reasons why a breached entity might be reluctant, or unable, to share the full details of a breach incident. Crisis comms teams may want to get some information out to customers once news of an incident surfaces, to preserve reputation and prevent harmful speculation from mounting. But they may not yet know the full picture.

Information such as exactly what was compromised and how may take weeks or even months to establish, especially if it involves large data volumes. And if there’s a chance that broader disclosure could help other threat actors (by revealing the attack path and defensive weaknesses) or the adversary itself (if it is still inside the network) then it may be withheld.

There are also more financially driven motives for limiting disclosure. Excessive info-sharing might impact the share price, reputation, and/or competitive advantage of an organization.

The truth is that disclosures to regulators will usually feature far more detail. The victims, meanwhile, are often left grasping at straws.

How do you interpret a breach notice?

The language used in a breach notification can be confusing. If it says your data was “accessed” it doesn’t necessarily mean it was actually stolen (i.e., “exfiltrated”). And just because a breached company claims they have seen “no evidence of misuse” there’s absolutely no guarantee that this is true. What they see and what’s actually happening on the cybercrime underground can be two very different things.

Similarly, if a company says you “may have been affected” it doesn’t mean your data was definitely in the trove that was compromised – although it’s always best to err on the side of caution.

As mentioned, breach notices may be cagey about exactly how the hackers got in and stole the data (the attack vector). But for victims, this is one of the less important pieces of information. What you really need to know is:

Whether your data was ‘only’ accessed or actually taken (although it’s best to assume the worst until you hear different)

What data was taken, as this will determine your next steps (e.g., whether you need to reset passwords, call your bank, cancel cards etc)

When the incident happened and how long it lasted, as this can help you to check against suspicious activity on affected accounts

What the company itself is telling you to do in terms of specific next steps

Is the notification even legitimate?

It’s also important to check if the notice is genuine. Scammers have grown wise to the fact that breach notifications are an increasingly common occurrence. And something that recipients are likely to take notice of and act on.

For that reason, you should never click through on any unsolicited breach notification email or message. Sometimes the stated incident might never have happened. On other occasions the original breach might be real but the notification message is a scam.

In any case, your first port of call should be to check with the breached organization. Do this not by replying to the message or using contact details listed there, but verifying them elsewhere.

What should happen next?

Once you’ve confirmed the notification is legitimate, ask the organization involved if it can clarify any more details. Then consider the following steps, which are dependent on the type of data that may have been compromised:

For personal details like email and home address, name and phone number, be on the lookout for follow-on phishing messages and calls. Never click on links in these messages or hand out information without verifying their authenticity separately

For health info or customer account details, watch out for more targeted phishing attempts as per the above

For usernames and passwords, change the credentials immediately for this account and anywhere else it was used. Switch on two-factor authentication (2FA) for an extra layer of security

For bank or card details, contact your bank or card provider and tell them what happened. Ask for a replacement card and monitor your accounts for suspicious activity

For government ID (e.g., passports, driver’s license) follow the advice of the issuer. A replacement may be needed

For financial and identity info, monitor your accounts, contact the relevant financial institution(s), change your logins (if relevant), and consider credit monitoring and a credit freeze

Is a credit freeze or credit monitoring the best option?

Many breached organizations offer free credit monitoring for a year following an incident. Some also offer a credit freeze. But which is better? It’s important to understand the difference.

Credit monitoring services detect when something changes on your credit file, potentially indicating a fraudster has your details and is trying to get a new line of credit out in your name.

Credit freeze blocks most access to your credit report, so scammers can’t easily open a new account using your details.

So a credit freeze is more useful, but if either is offered, take advantage of them. The two work best together: place a freeze and accept any free monitoring you’re offered. Just be aware that credit monitoring is only an alert service. It won’t actually prevent follow-on fraud.

As more of us expand the number of organizations we do business with, and as hackers get better at compromising those same companies, the odds of receiving a breach notification will continue to shorten. But it doesn’t have to be the end of the world. Stay alert and stay informed to minimize the risk of follow-on fraud.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

How do I know if a breach notification is genuine or a scam?

Never click through on any unsolicited breach notification email or message. Check first with the breached organization, and not by replying to the message or using contact details listed there, but verifying independently.

Why have I received a breach notification from a company I’ve never heard of?

It may be a supplier you’ve never dealt with directly, such as a payroll provider or data processor used by a company you do business with. It may also be a scam, or you may simply not have done business with them for a long time and it could be a historic breach. Either way, read the information carefully and contact the company directly for more information if it looks like sensitive financial or personal information was exposed.

What should I do if my password was exposed in a breach?

Change the credentials immediately for this account and anywhere else it was used. Switch on two-factor authentication (2FA) for an extra layer of security.

What should I do if my financial details and identity information were exposed in a breach?

This is more serious. Monitor any relevant accounts for suspicious activity and contact the relevant financial institution(s). Change your logins (if relevant) and consider credit monitoring and a credit freeze.

Should I use credit monitoring after a breach?

Credit monitoring services detect when something changes on your credit file, potentially indicating a fraudster has your details and is trying to get a new line of credit out in your name. It won’t actually prevent follow-on fraud, but it can be a useful alerting mechanism. If offered for free, accept it. A credit freeze is worth adding: it’s free in the US and blocks most access to your credit report.

Title: MATCHBOIL: New tricks, same old evil intentions

Full Text:
ESET researchers have documented the evolution of the MATCHBOIL malware, a custom C# downloader wielded by the Russia-aligned UAC-0099 APT group. The malware is used to download a payload from the group’s C&C server, install it, and establish its persistence. Although MATCHBOIL was first documented by CERT-UA in August 2025, our research indicates that it has been in development since at least 2024. The earliest versions of the malware that we analyzed are from April 2024 and the latest from April 2026. This blogpost goes over these versions chronologically and describes the malware’s changes. Each new iteration of the downloader was more sophisticated than the last, showing that MATCHBOIL is an important part of UAC-0099’s toolkit.

Key points of the blogpost:

MATCHBOIL is a C# downloader used by the Russia-aligned group UAC‑0099 to download, install, and persist another payload.

The analyzed MATCHBOIL versions show a change in code obfuscation from originally using Unicode symbol renaming to now employing the Eziriz .NET Reactor obfuscator.

Various techniques to determine whether it is being executed in a sandboxed environment have been implemented in MATCHBOIL over time.

Although MATCHBOIL was first documented by CERT-UA in August 2025, we believe that, based on the compilation timestamps of some discovered samples, MATCHBOIL could have been in development since April 2024.

Our investigation into the various MATCHBOIL versions started in February 2026, when two samples related to the malware were uploaded to VirusTotal. Since both samples establish communication with a domain previously attributed to UAC‑0099, we decided to take a closer look. That led us to discover (in ESET telemetry) samples with similar malicious behavior, dating from November and December 2025. We believe that all these samples are variants of MATCHBOIL.

Further research revealed even older samples, compiled in April 2024 and seen in ESET telemetry in July and August 2025. The timestamps found in the first publicly known MATCHBOIL samples that CERT‑UA documented in August 2025 indicate that those samples were also built in the middle of 2024, meaning that UAC‑0099 was likely already developing MATCHBOIL at that time.

From all the samples of the downloader that we collected, we see that UAC‑0099 is continually improving MATCHBOIL for future attacks – the samples compiled or seen before November 2025 were much more straightforward and simple to analyze compared to newer ones.

All the MACTHBOIL victims that we have seen in our telemetry were in Ukraine, across various sectors. From July to August 2025, we saw samples of the downloader at multiple transportation companies. In December of the same year, they were seen at a manufacturing company. Later, in June 2026, ESET telemetry registered further MATCHBOIL samples, this time at a company in the energy sector.

The two samples that were found on VirusTotal in February 2026 had also been uploaded from Ukraine.

UAC-0099 profile

UAC‑0099 is a cyberespionage group targeting governmental organizations, financial institutions, and media, all in Ukraine. Based on the targeting, we believe with medium confidence that the group is aligned with Russian interests. UAC-0099 can act as an initial access broker for Sandworm, a Russia-aligned group best known for its destructive attacks in Ukraine.

The group has been active since at least 2022 and was first reported by CERT-UA in June 2023. Apart from MATCHBOIL, the group also typically deploys LONEPAGE, a PowerShell downloader named after the presence of the word page in its C&C URLs.

MATCHBOIL 101

MATCHBOIL is a C# downloader whose purpose is to download another payload from its C&C server, install it, and then establish its persistence.

The malware is distributed via malicious links in spearphishing emails. Clicking the link downloads an archive file with a VBScript file payload that downloads and executes MATCHBOIL on the victim machine. Note that for the malicious payload to take effect, the victim is misled into executing the script manually.

At runtime, MATCHBOIL checks for the existence of a specific directory (the name of which varies with each sample) located in %LOCALAPPDATA%. The directory is used to install the payload on the victim’s machine; if the directory already exists, the malware terminates. During execution, MATCHBOIL obtains the CPUID, BIOS serial number, and other basic information about the victim machine, which is used to identify the victim during C&C communication.

MATCHBOIL then performs three HTTPS requests to the C&C server; each with a different purpose:

The first request receives a numeric value from the C&C server. MATCHBOIL uses it for the second request as a value in one of its HTTP headers; the name of this HTTP header varies with the sample. It is possible that this numeric value is used to indicate which payload must be downloaded from the C&C server.

The C&C server response to the second request is a piece of code, expected to be formatted as HTML. Embedded within the code is a hex-encoded payload that gets installed on the victim’s machine. To extract the payload from the response, MATCHBOIL uses a regular expression pattern, which is, again, sample dependent. Once the payload is extracted, it is decoded from hex into bytes. We have seen different regular expressions being used over time, but most contain an HTML tag format, for example <script>(.*?)</script>.

The third request receives a string from the C&C server that is saved into a file in the same directory where the payload is installed. The file can act as the payload’s configuration. As with the previous requests, the name of this file varies based on the sample.

From our analysis, we have discovered that in most cases, the hex-encoded payload to be installed on the victim machine is a C# backdoor known as MATCHWOK, used exclusively by UAC-0099 and firstly documented by CERT‑UA.

Once communication with the C&C server has finished, MATCHBOIL persists the installed payload, a PE file, for later execution. The persistence mechanism can be set up via scheduled tasks or by adding a value to the Windows registry.

Persistence for MATCHBOIL itself is established by the VBScript used to download and install the malware. We found a related VBScript sample lately in ESET telemetry that persists a C# loader that executes MATCHBOIL.

MATCHBOIL’s configuration is hardcoded within the samples, containing the strings related to C&C communication, directories, and filenames to be installed on the victim machine. The first samples contained these strings encrypted in the binary, but the latest one contains them in clear text or encrypted because of the obfuscator .NET Reactor.

The evolution of MATCHBOIL

We analyzed MATCHBOIL samples that appeared over an almost two-year period, from those with timestamps from April 2024 to those discovered in April 2026. In this relatively short time span, we saw UAC-0099 make many improvements to the downloader’s code, with the main changes concerning the following:

Overall logic switching from a one-shot downloader executed only once to, at the end of 2025, being executed on a two-minute timer, becoming able to retrieve the latest payload from the C&C.

Obfuscation – going from using unprintable Unicode characters and string encryption algorithms to the Eziriz .NET Reactor obfuscator.

Persistence mechanism – moving from using a combination of a specific registry value and a scheduled task (2024), to using a Windows registry value in the Run key exclusively (July 2025), to a scheduled task (late 2025).

Defense evasion – gradually, starting in the late 2025, adding methods to check whether the malware is running in a sandbox environment.

User deception – starting in late 2025, adding a graphical user interface (GUI) that appears if the user executes the payload and changed it to a less conspicuous version in early 2026.

In the next sections, we go over all the observed MATCHBOIL versions chronologically, based on their compilation timestamps, and describe them in detail. Despite the continuous changes to the malware’s code, its task remains the same: download and persist a payload from the C&C.

2024 samples

The earliest MATCHBOIL samples that we have seen have compilation timestamps from 2024.

All the C# class and method names in these samples were obfuscated using unprintable Unicode symbols, e.g., \uFDD1.\uFDD0. The strings in the binaries are encrypted with a custom encryption algorithm that is a combination of the XOR operation with bitwise shifts using a numeric seed for decrypting the string. This seed varies with the sample.

Figure 1 shows the decompiled version of the string decryption algorithm used by MATCHBOIL samples from this period.

As we previously mentioned, MATCHBOIL retrieves information from the victim machine, which serves to identify it during C&C communication. Using the C# class ManagementObjectSearcher, it performs different Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) queries, and retrieves, for example, the CPUID of the victim machine or the BIOS serial number. Figure 2 shows a decompiled version of the logic used to retrieve this information. Later versions of MATCHBOIL obtain more information about the victim, such as the username and the MAC address of the network interface.

As described in the MATCHBOIL 101 section: before C&C communication starts, the malware checks whether the payload is already installed on the victim’s machine. It does so by checking for both the existence of the directory used for installing the payload, and the payload itself.

If the payload is not present, MATCHBOIL starts C&C communication, which consists of three HTTPS requests to the C&C server. In the case of the 2024 samples, the malware uses a custom HTTP header named SN (possibly for serial number) containing the previously obtained victim information, and an HTTP header named User-Agent, filled with a 25-character-long string that can contain special characters.

When the first request is executed, the C&C server responds with a numeric value that is used in the second request as the value of another specific HTTP header, this one named Count. This value seems to be an ID that the C&C server can use to identify which payload to download to the victim machine, and/or to validate that the request came from MATCHBOIL and no other service.

Based on the malware’s logic, the response of the C&C server to the second request is expected to be formatted as HTML code that contains the payload hex encoded. MATCHBOIL retrieves the payload from the response body and then installs it under the specified directory with a specific, hardcoded filename. For the 2024 samples, the exact path was %LOCALAPPDATA%\DeviceMonitor.

The third request retrieves a string that is saved in a file named config.ini in the same directory where the payload is installed. It is most probably a configuration file for the payload.

Once the C&C communication is finished, MATCHBOIL sets up the payload’s persistence on the victim machine. In the analyzed 2024 samples, MATCHBOIL achieves persistence in two ways: creating a registry value named DeviceMonitor under the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key and a scheduled task named Updates\CheckTask.

Finally, all the logic mentioned in this section is located inside a C# main class. In this version, MATCHBOIL works as a one‑shot downloader and relies on its persistence mechanisms to execute the installed payload.

July 2025 samples

There aren’t many significant changes between the samples from July 2025 and the ones from 2024.

The biggest change in the malware’s logic is that the code is executed via asynchronous tasks using the Task library. This means that the execution of the next task doesn’t proceed until the previous task finishes, e.g., when MATCHBOIL makes the first request to the C&C, it doesn’t proceed to the second one until the first is done.

As opposed to the 2024 samples, this version of MATCHBOIL obtains more information about the victim’s machine for the SN HTTP header: the serial number of the BIOS, the physical address of the first or default network interface, and the model and manufacturer of the computer.

When it comes to persistence, this time, it is achieved via Windows registry entries in the Run key.

The last noteworthy modification in these samples of MATCHBOIL is that the malware executes the payload after its installation by creating a Win32_Process object via ManagementClass.

November and December 2025 samples

The samples documented in this section were discovered in ESET telemetry in November and December 2025. While these samples have invalid timestamps, our analysis strongly suggests they are newer than the samples from July 2025, since they display major changes compared to that version.

First, instead of using obfuscation methods based on unprintable Unicode symbols and string encryption, UAC‑0099 has replaced them with the Eziriz .NET Reactor obfuscator. This obfuscator has multiple features such as code virtualization and control flow obfuscation, which can make the analysis of MATCHBOIL more complex.

To further disguise the malware, the operators have also introduced a graphical user interface (GUI) in the form of a daily planner that is shown to the victims if they execute MATCHBOIL manually. As can be seen in Figure 3, the strength of this ruse is somewhat lessened by the appearance of this “planner”, the presence of two text fields both titled Today, as well as by a typo in the window name that suggests the program should be used to plan one’s milk product intake.

In order to execute its malicious activity, this version of MATCHBOIL expects to be started with the argument ‑auto. If this argument is not present, it means that the malware was executed manually, and the GUI is displayed to the victim. If the argument is present, MATCHBOIL proceeds to create a mutex named Global\PlannerAssistant. Perhaps to go with the theming of the GUI program, the payload of the late 2025 samples is installed under %LOCALAPPDATA%\MeowCheck\ and has the filename MeowMeowProgramm.exe.

After creating the mutex, MATCHBOIL determines whether it is running in a sandboxed or other dedicated analysis environment by using the query *[System/EventID=6013] via the .NET class EventLogReader to obtain Windows event logs. The events logged under ID 6013 report how long the system has been running since the last boot. MATCHBOIL has two regular expressions that it uses for iterating over these logs to try to obtain the uptime of the victim machine:

uptime\sis\s(\d+)\sseconds

работоспособного\sсостояния\s(\d+)\sсек

The second regular expression is written in Russian, which machine translates to operational\sstate\s(\d+)\ssec.

If MATCHBOIL detects that there are at least three events with an uptime value at least of 7,200 seconds, which is equal to two hours, then MATCHBOIL assumes that it is not running in a sandbox or other dedicated analysis machine.

It also checks whether it is attached to a debugger by checking the property IsAttached from the .NET class Debugger. If not, it creates a timer that runs MATCHBOIL’s C&C communication logic every two minutes. This is an interesting modification in MATCHBOIL’s logic because it changes the one-shot downloader behavior. Now it can maintain communication with the C&C server, allowing it to download the latest available payload or, if there is an issue in the first communication with the C&C server, MATCHBOIL can retrieve its payload from the C&C server with later requests.

Once these checks are done, MATCHBOIL proceeds to execute the usual three requests to the C&C server using the same HTTP headers SN and User-Agent, with the exception that in the second request, the HTTP header used for the numeric value is Answer.

In some of these samples (for example SHA‑1: F886B615CB9E23EAD2718FF2A61155ACFB04CE9E), the logic used for C&C communication, and for persisting and retrieving the payload from the HTML code, is located in a DLL named AdditionalLib.dll. It is installed in the directory where MATCHBOIL is located.

Figure 4 shows, at the top, the decompiled code of the second HTTPS request used in this batch of MATCHBOIL samples, and at the bottom the same HTTPS request from an older sample from 2024. Note that the code has been deobfuscated.

We have also seen that MATCHBOIL saves the payload from the second request to a temporary file named WallpappersSet.jpg, in the directory C:\Users\<username>\Pictures.

The response from the third request is saved in a file named config.library-ms under the directory C:\Users\Public\Libraries. In older samples this response was saved in the same directory where the payload was installed, with the filename config.ini.

The persistence mechanism of the payload also changed, showing that the group is constantly switching from one specific mechanism to another. In this version, the malware creates a scheduled task named UpdateCheckers\DailyPlanner that runs every seven minutes.

2026 samples

We have found several distinct MATCHBOIL samples so far in 2026. In February, we first discovered a sample (SHA‑1: 1E2C4AAC30EDFF86CD9A30BD08B199BCD3D0CCCE) with mostly minor changes compared to the previous version. One such change is an adjustment to the check of whether MATCHBOIL should run its malicious code: the operators have added the argument ‑plans that is executed along with the previous one, ‑auto.

Later in the same month, we discovered another sample (SHA‑1: C85D28F7D272CE2BBBFB9DAE71D21BF25B8D00FC). In this one, the argument used to execute the malicious activity is ‑renew; if this argument is not present or is different, then MATCHBOIL displays the GUI that is shown in Figure 5. This time, it is a utility that can search within text files based on regular expressions or a pattern provided by the user, showing that the operators have seemingly moved beyond the daily planner from Figure 3.

The most recent variant that we have discovered in 2026 comes from April and has the SHA‑1: 050926727CDD74F0B3A8A098E60B76D10FB06B14. It constitutes the first time that a MATCHBOIL sample is a DLL file executed by a custom C# loader; all previous samples were EXE files that sometimes came with a DLL containing a portion of the malware’s logic. CERT-UA has also described this variant, naming it MATCHBOIL.V2.

This newest variant adds another check to determine whether it is running in a virtual environment: it checks if the installation date of the operating system is 10 or more days older than the date on which the MATCHBOIL sample is being executed. As previously mentioned, if true then MATCHBOIL terminates.

In this version of the malware, the downloaded payload is installed under the directory %LOCALAPPDATA%\SMTPClient in a file named SMTPClientApplication.exe. If we compare this directory and filename with the ones used at the end of 2025, there is an attempt at disguising the payload on the victim machine, since SMTPClientApplication.exe stands out much less than a program file named MeowMeowProgramm.exe.

As a persistence mechanism, the malware uses a scheduled task named Checker under a directory named MailClient.

Other MATCHBOIL logic that we had mentioned in previous samples, such as logic to obtain information from the victim machine and regular expressions to obtain the payload and its potential configuration, is largely unchanged.

Network infrastructure

UAC‑0099 uses virtual private servers such as BitLaunch to host its C&C servers, and cloud services such as Cloudflare to hide the servers. These servers use HTTP and HTTPS. We have also seen that the TLS certificates were generated with Let’s Encrypt, and that the certificates are not reused on other domains.

Conclusion

Our investigation of MATCHBOIL samples from April 2024 to April 2026 revealed multiple modifications, from code level structure to the use of the .NET Reactor obfuscator, all of these implemented in a relatively short time. This demonstrates a keen interest by UAC-0099 operators in improving their downloader, not only to avoid detection by security solutions, but also to use it as a key part of their toolset in future attacks.
